notes.front: What is adjusted gross income (AGI)?
notes.back: The income figure you reach before subtracting the deductions used to figure taxable income (the standard deduction or itemized deductions).
notes.explanation: Pub. 17 places the standard deduction and itemized deductions after AGI: they are subtracted from it, not from gross income.
notes.example: Like a subtotal on a bill: taxable income is what remains once the deductions come off it.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Standard Deduction”, PDF p. 94
notes.evidence: After you have figured your adjusted gross income, you are ready to subtract the deductions used to figure taxable income

notes.front: What is the standard deduction?
notes.back: A dollar amount that reduces taxable income, taken instead of listing actual deductible expenses.
notes.explanation: Pub. 17 says it spares many taxpayers the need to itemize actual deductions.
notes.example: Like a flat expense allowance offered instead of adding up receipts.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Standard Deduction”, PDF p. 94
notes.evidence: The standard deduction is a dollar amount that reduces your taxable income. It is a benefit that eliminates the need for many taxpayers to itemize actual deductions

notes.front: What are itemized deductions, and where are they claimed?
notes.back: Deductions for particular expenses, listed on Schedule A (Form 1040) instead of taking the standard deduction.
notes.explanation: A taxpayer either takes the standard deduction or itemizes on Schedule A; the 2025 Schedule 1-A deductions are the exception, open to both.
notes.example: Like handing in each receipt instead of taking the flat allowance.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: New deductions for itemizers and non-itemizers”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: you can claim these deductions if you take the standard deduction or if you itemize on Schedule A (Form 1040)

notes.front: In Pub. 936, what are points?
notes.back: Certain charges paid, or treated as paid, by a borrower to obtain a home mortgage.
notes.explanation: The same charges may appear on closing papers under another name, loan origination fees.
notes.example: Like a fee a bank charges up front to set up a loan, but tied to a mortgage on your home.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Points”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: The term "points" is used to describe certain charges paid, or treated as paid, by a borrower to obtain a home mortgage.

notes.front: What is home acquisition debt?
notes.back: A mortgage taken out to buy, build or substantially improve your home.
notes.explanation: Pub. 936 uses the name for mortgages of that purpose; a loan spent on something else is not home acquisition debt.
notes.example: Like the loan a family takes to build a new kitchen extension, as opposed to one they spend on a holiday.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Part I: Fully deductible interest”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: took out after December 15, 2017, to buy, build, or substantially improve your home (called home acquisition debt)

notes.front: What are qualified tips?
notes.back: Voluntary tips set by the customer, paid in cash, by card or cheque, in an occupation customarily tipped by 31 December 2024.
notes.explanation: Tips outside this definition, such as tips that are negotiated or not paid voluntarily, don’t count towards the 2025 tips deduction.
notes.example: Like a waiter’s tips reported for 2025, which may now reduce taxable income instead of only adding to it.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Schedule 1-A, Part II: Qualified tips”, PDF p. 101
notes.evidence: Qualified tips are tips that you received from customers or, as an employee, through a tip-sharing arrangement in an occupation that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024.

notes.front: What is qualified overtime compensation?
notes.back: The part of overtime pay required by the Fair Labor Standards Act that is above your regular rate: generally the “half” of “time-and-a-half”.
notes.explanation: Only that premium counts for the 2025 Schedule 1-A overtime deduction; the regular-rate part of overtime pay, and extra pay above time-and-a-half, stay fully taxable.
notes.example: Like a worker paid $30 an hour instead of $20 for an extra hour over 40 in a workweek: only the extra $10 is qualified overtime.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Schedule 1-A, Part III: Qualified overtime compensation”, PDF p. 106
notes.evidence: Qualified overtime compensation means overtime compensation that is paid to you as required under section 7 of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA) that is more than the amount of your regular rate of pay.

notes.front: What is a nonrefundable credit?
notes.back: A credit that can reduce your tax to zero, but whose excess over your tax is not refunded to you.
notes.explanation: Pub. 970 uses the lifetime learning credit to illustrate this kind of credit.
notes.example: Like a voucher that can bring a bill down to nothing but never pays you change.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Lifetime Learning Credit”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: This means that it can reduce your tax to zero, but if the credit is more than your tax, the excess won't be refunded to you.

notes.front: What is a refundable credit (or refundable portion of a credit)?
notes.back: One whose excess over your tax is refunded to you.
notes.explanation: Pub. 970 illustrates it with the part of the American opportunity credit that may be refundable.
notes.example: Like a voucher worth more than the bill, where the shop pays you the difference in cash.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “American Opportunity Credit”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: This means that if the refundable portion of your credit is more than your tax, the excess will be refunded to you.

notes.front: What is the child tax credit (CTC), and on which schedule is it figured?
notes.back: A credit for each qualifying child, figured on Schedule 8812 (Form 1040).
notes.explanation: The same schedule also figures the credit for other dependents and the additional child tax credit.
notes.example: Like a per-child allowance taken off the family’s tax bill.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “Purpose of Schedule”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Use Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) to figure your child tax credit (CTC), credit for other dependents (ODC), and additional child tax credit (ACTC).

notes.front: What is the additional child tax credit (ACTC)?
notes.back: The refund-producing part of the child credit, figured on Schedule 8812; returns claiming it get refunds no earlier than mid-February.
notes.explanation: Returns that properly claim it get no refund before mid-February 2026.
notes.example: Like the change a shop hands back when a voucher is worth more than the bill.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “Reminders: Delayed refund for returns claiming ACTC”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The IRS can't issue refunds before mid-February 2026 for returns that properly claim ACTC.

notes.front: What is the credit for other dependents (ODC)?
notes.back: A credit that may reduce your tax by up to $500 for each eligible dependent.
notes.explanation: Pub. 17 warns that it and the child tax credit are separate from the child and dependent care credit.
notes.example: Like the child tax credit, but for dependents who don’t qualify for it, such as a dependent parent.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Child Tax Credit and Credit for Other Dependents”, PDF p. 111
notes.evidence: The ODC is a credit that may reduce your tax by as much as $500 for each eligible dependent.

notes.front: What is the American opportunity credit (AOTC)?
notes.back: An education credit for a student who had not completed the first four years of postsecondary education before 2025.
notes.explanation: Pub. 970 describes it as generally covering the freshman to senior years.
notes.example: Like a scholarship paid through the tax return, but only for undergraduate-level years.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Table 2-1. Overview of the American Opportunity Credit”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: available only if the student had not completed the first 4 years of postsecondary education before 2025

notes.front: What is the lifetime learning credit (LLC)?
notes.back: An education credit for qualified education expenses that can be claimed for a student for any number of years.
notes.explanation: Unlike the American opportunity credit, it has no four-year cap.
notes.example: Like the American opportunity credit, but open to a graduate student or an adult taking a course in any year.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Lifetime Learning Credit”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: There is no limit on the number of years the lifetime learning credit can be claimed for each student.

notes.front: What is the foreign tax credit (FTC)?
notes.back: A credit for qualified foreign income taxes that reduces your United States tax liability, instead of only your taxable income.
notes.explanation: Pub. 514 contrasts it with taking the same taxes as a deduction, which reduces taxable income instead.
notes.example: Like being allowed to count tax already paid to France against your tax bill at home.
notes.source: Publication 514 (2025), Foreign Tax Credit for Individuals, “Introduction”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Taken as a deduction, foreign income taxes reduce your U.S. taxable income. Taken as a credit, foreign income taxes reduce your U.S. tax liability.

notes.front: What is the earned income credit (EIC)?
notes.back: A tax credit for certain people who work and have earned income under $68,675 (2025).
notes.explanation: The $68,675 ceiling is the highest limit, for married couples with three or more children; the limits for others are lower.
notes.example: Like a wage top-up for low and moderate earners, paid through the tax return.
notes.source: Publication 596 (2025), Earned Income Credit, “Introduction”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: The EIC is a tax credit for certain people who work and have earned income under $68,675.

notes.front: What is the premium tax credit (PTC)?
notes.back: A tax credit for certain people who enroll, or whose family member enrolls, in a qualified health plan through a Marketplace.
notes.explanation: It helps pay the premiums for that health plan.
notes.example: Like a subsidy on health insurance bought through the government exchange.
notes.source: Publication 974 (2025), Premium Tax Credit, “What Is the Premium Tax Credit (PTC)?”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The PTC is a tax credit for certain people who enroll, or whose family member enrolls, in a qualified health plan offered through a Marketplace.

notes.front: What are advance payments of the premium tax credit (APTC)?
notes.back: Payments made during the year to your insurer toward the premiums of a qualified health plan, based on the Marketplace’s estimate of your credit.
notes.explanation: Pub. 974 says APTC eligibility rests on the Marketplace’s estimate of the credit.
introduces: advance payments of the premium tax credit
notes.example: Like a monthly discount on a premium that is settled up at the end of the year.
notes.source: Publication 974 (2025), Premium Tax Credit, “Advance payments of the premium tax credit (APTC)”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The APTC is a payment made during the year to your insurance provider that pays for part or all of the premiums for a qualified health plan
uses: advance payments of the premium tax credit

notes.front: What is Form 1095-A?
notes.back: The Health Insurance Marketplace Statement, sent by the Marketplace to people enrolled through it.
notes.explanation: Pub. 974 tells people who don’t receive it, or think it is wrong, to contact their Marketplace.
notes.example: Like an annual statement from a lender, but from the health insurance Marketplace.
notes.source: Publication 974 (2025), Premium Tax Credit, “Useful Items”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Contact your Marketplace if you do not receive a Form 1095-A or if you have questions about the accuracy of your Form 1095-A.

notes.front: What is qualified business income (QBI)?
notes.back: The qualified items of income, gain, deduction and loss from your trades or businesses: the base for the QBI deduction.
notes.explanation: The deduction on it is figured on Form 8995 or Form 8995-A.
notes.example: Like the profit of a sole proprietor’s bakery, which may earn a deduction of its own.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025), Qualified Business Income Deduction Simplified Computation, “Determining Your Qualified Business Income”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Your QBI includes qualified items of income, gain, deduction, and loss from your trades or businesses

notes.front: For 2025, the standard deduction for a single filer, or someone married filing separately, is {{c1::$15,750}}.
notes.explanation: Pub. 17 lists it among the 2025 increases, which apply to all filers.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Standard deduction amount increased”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The amounts are: • Single or married filing separately—$15,750;

notes.front: For 2025, the standard deduction for married filing jointly, or a qualifying surviving spouse, is {{c1::$31,500}}.
notes.explanation: The joint amount is twice the single amount.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Standard deduction amount increased”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: • Married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse—$31,500;

notes.front: For 2025, the standard deduction for head of household is {{c1::$23,625}}.
notes.explanation: It sits between the single ($15,750) and joint ($31,500) amounts.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Standard deduction amount increased”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: • Head of household—$23,625. See chapter 10, later.

notes.front: A married couple filing jointly has $28,000 of itemized deductions for 2025. Which should they take?
notes.back: B: the $31,500 standard deduction.
notes.choices:
A) Itemized deductions of $28,000
B) The standard deduction of $31,500
C) Half of each
notes.choicesExplained: A is $3,500 smaller. C: a return takes either the standard deduction or itemized deductions, not a mix.
notes.explanation: $31,500 − $28,000 = $3,500 more from the standard deduction.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Standard deduction amount increased”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: • Married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse—$31,500;

notes.front: A head of household has $19,000 of itemized deductions for 2025. Which deduction is larger?
notes.back: B: the $23,625 standard deduction for head of household.
notes.choices:
A) Itemized, $19,000
B) Standard, $23,625
C) Standard, $15,750
notes.choicesExplained: A is $4,625 smaller. C is the single amount, not the head of household amount.
notes.explanation: $23,625 − $19,000 = $4,625 more from the standard deduction.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Standard deduction amount increased”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: • Head of household—$23,625. See chapter 10, later.

notes.front: When is a married person filing separately’s standard deduction zero?
notes.back: When their spouse itemizes deductions on their own return.
notes.explanation: In that case Pub. 17 says to itemize any deductions you have.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Persons not eligible for the standard deduction”, PDF p. 94
notes.evidence: Your standard deduction is zero and you should itemize any deductions you have if: • Your filing status is married filing separately, and your spouse itemizes deductions on their return;

notes.front: Ravi and Mei file separate 2025 returns. Mei itemizes. Ravi has $3,000 of deductible expenses. What can Ravi deduct?
notes.back: B: his standard deduction is zero, so he itemizes his $3,000.
notes.choices:
A) The $15,750 standard deduction
B) His $3,000 of itemized deductions
C) Nothing at all
notes.choicesExplained: A: the standard deduction is zero when the spouse itemizes. C: he can still itemize what he has.
notes.explanation: Because Mei itemizes, Ravi’s standard deduction is zero; itemizing gives $3,000.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Persons not eligible for the standard deduction”, PDF p. 94
notes.evidence: Your standard deduction is zero and you should itemize any deductions you have if: • Your filing status is married filing separately, and your spouse itemizes deductions on their return;

notes.front: For 2025, an unmarried taxpayer who is 65 or older or blind adds {{c1::$2,000}} to the standard deduction for each of those conditions.
notes.explanation: The worksheet multiplies the amount by the number of boxes checked, so 65 and blind together count twice.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 8. Standard Deduction Worksheet for Dependents”, PDF p. 26
notes.evidence: If born before January 2, 1961, or blind, multiply $2,000 ($1,600 if married) by the number in the box above.

notes.front: For 2025, a married taxpayer who is 65 or older or blind adds {{c1::$1,600}} to the standard deduction for each condition.
notes.explanation: Married taxpayers get a smaller add-on than unmarried ones ($2,000).
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 8. Standard Deduction Worksheet for Dependents”, PDF p. 26
notes.evidence: If born before January 2, 1961, or blind, multiply $2,000 ($1,600 if married) by the number in the box above.

notes.front: Grace is single, 70 and blind, and cannot be claimed as a dependent. What is her 2025 standard deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves out both add-ons. B counts only one of her two conditions.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 8. Standard Deduction Worksheet for Dependents”, PDF p. 26
notes.evidence: If born before January 2, 1961, or blind, multiply $2,000 ($1,600 if married) by the number in the box above.

notes.front: A couple files jointly for 2025. One spouse is 68 and blind; the other is 50 and not blind. What is their standard deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves out the add-ons. B counts only one of the two conditions.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 8. Standard Deduction Worksheet for Dependents”, PDF p. 26
notes.evidence: If born before January 2, 1961, or blind, multiply $2,000 ($1,600 if married) by the number in the box above.

notes.front: What is the 2025 standard deduction for someone who can be claimed as a dependent?
notes.back: Generally the greater of $1,350, or earned income plus $450, but no more than the regular standard deduction.
notes.explanation: It can be higher if the dependent is 65 or older or blind.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Standard Deduction for Dependents”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: is generally limited to the greater of: 1. $1,350, or 2. The individual's earned income for the year plus $450 (but not more than the regular standard deduction amount, generally $15,750).

notes.front: Lena, 17, is her parents’ dependent. In 2025 she earned $4,000 of wages and had no other income. What is her standard deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: A is the floor, used only when it is larger. B forgets the $450.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Standard Deduction for Dependents”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: is generally limited to the greater of: 1. $1,350, or 2. The individual's earned income for the year plus $450

notes.front: Which new 2025 schedule to Form 1040 holds the deductions for tips, overtime, car loan interest and seniors?
notes.back: Schedule 1-A.
notes.explanation: It was created for the four deductions enacted in 2025.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: New Schedule 1-A”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: A new schedule to Form 1040, Schedule 1-A, has been created for taxpayers to claim a deduction for the recently enacted deductions for no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on car loan interest, and the enhanced senior deduction.

notes.front: Must a taxpayer itemize to claim the four new Schedule 1-A deductions?
notes.back: No: they can be claimed with the standard deduction or when itemizing.
notes.explanation: Pub. 17 calls them new deductions for itemizers and non-itemizers.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: New deductions for itemizers and non-itemizers”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: you can claim these deductions if you take the standard deduction or if you itemize on Schedule A (Form 1040)

notes.front: Dana takes the 2025 standard deduction and received $8,000 of qualified tips. Can Dana also deduct the tips?
notes.back: C: yes, on Schedule 1-A, alongside the standard deduction.
notes.choices:
A) Only on Schedule A
B) No, only itemizers can
C) Yes, on Schedule 1-A
notes.choicesExplained: B and A: the Schedule 1-A deductions don’t depend on itemizing.
notes.explanation: The four new deductions are open to itemizers and non-itemizers alike.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: New deductions for itemizers and non-itemizers”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: you can claim these deductions if you take the standard deduction or if you itemize on Schedule A (Form 1040)

notes.front: For 2025, you can’t deduct more than {{c1::$25,000}} of qualified tips.
notes.explanation: The limit is on the tips themselves; income can reduce it further.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on tips”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: You can't deduct more than $25,000 of those tips.

notes.front: Above what modified AGI is the 2025 qualified tips deduction limited?
notes.back: $150,000 ($300,000 if married filing jointly).
notes.explanation: Below that level the deduction is not reduced for income.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on tips”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Your deduction will be limited if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $150,000 ($300,000 if married filing jointly). To be eligible, you and/or your spouse who received the tips

notes.front: What two conditions does Pub. 17 set for the tips deduction, besides having qualified tips?
notes.back: A valid social security number for whoever received the tips, and, if married, a joint return.
notes.explanation: The same two conditions apply to the overtime deduction.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on tips”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: To be eligible, you and/or your spouse who received the tips must have a valid social security number (SSN). If you are married, you must file a joint return.

notes.front: Sofia, single with a valid social security number and modified AGI of $62,000, received $31,000 of qualified tips in 2025. What is her tips deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the $25,000 cap. C: she meets the conditions and is under the $150,000 income level.
notes.explanation: Smaller of $31,000 tips or the $25,000 cap = $25,000; $62,000 is below $150,000, so no reduction.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on tips”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: You can't deduct more than $25,000 of those tips.

notes.front: Kofi is married and received qualified tips in 2025. He and his wife file separate returns. Can he take the tips deduction?
notes.back: A: no; a married taxpayer must file a joint return to take it.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, up to $12,500
C) Yes, up to $25,000
notes.choicesExplained: C and B: no amount is allowed on a separate return.
notes.explanation: Pub. 17 makes a joint return a condition for married taxpayers.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on tips”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: To be eligible, you and/or your spouse who received the tips must have a valid social security number (SSN). If you are married, you must file a joint return.

notes.front: A single bartender has $170,000 of modified AGI and $20,000 of qualified tips. What happens to the tips deduction?
notes.back: C: it is limited, because modified AGI exceeds $150,000.
notes.choices:
A) It is allowed in full
B) It is lost because the tips are under $25,000
C) It is limited
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the income limit. B: being under the cap does not remove the deduction.
notes.explanation: $170,000 is more than the $150,000 single threshold, so the deduction is reduced.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on tips”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Your deduction will be limited if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $150,000 ($300,000 if married filing jointly).

notes.front: For 2025, the qualified overtime deduction is up to {{c1::$12,500}} for a single filer.
notes.explanation: Married couples filing jointly get twice this.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on overtime”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: you may be eligible to deduct up to $12,500 ($25,000 if married filing jointly) of your qualified overtime compensation.

notes.front: For 2025, the qualified overtime deduction for married filing jointly is up to {{c1::$25,000}}.
notes.explanation: It is double the $12,500 limit for other filers.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on overtime”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: you may be eligible to deduct up to $12,500 ($25,000 if married filing jointly) of your qualified overtime compensation.

notes.front: Above what modified AGI is the 2025 overtime deduction limited?
notes.back: $150,000 ($300,000 if married filing jointly).
notes.explanation: These are the same income levels as for the tips deduction.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on overtime”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: of your qualified overtime compensation. Your deduction will be limited if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $150,000 ($300,000 if married filing jointly).

notes.front: Liam is single, with modified AGI of $80,000 and $14,000 of qualified overtime compensation for 2025. What is his overtime deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the cap. C is the joint limit.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on overtime”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: you may be eligible to deduct up to $12,500 ($25,000 if married filing jointly) of your qualified overtime compensation.

notes.front: A couple filing jointly, modified AGI $140,000, has $20,000 of qualified overtime compensation between them. What is their overtime deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: A is the single limit. C is the cap, but they only have $20,000 of overtime.
notes.explanation: Smaller of $20,000 or the $25,000 joint cap = $20,000; $140,000 is under $300,000.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on overtime”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: you may be eligible to deduct up to $12,500 ($25,000 if married filing jointly) of your qualified overtime compensation.

notes.front: A couple filing jointly has modified AGI of $320,000 and $18,000 of qualified overtime. What happens to their overtime deduction?
notes.back: B: limited, since $320,000 exceeds the $300,000 joint threshold.
notes.choices:
A) Allowed in full
B) Limited
C) Not allowed because they file jointly
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the income limit. C: filing jointly is required, not a bar.
notes.explanation: $320,000 − $300,000 = $20,000 over the joint threshold, so the deduction is reduced.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on overtime”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Your deduction will be limited if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $150,000 ($300,000 if married filing jointly). To be eligible, you and/or your spouse who received the overtime

notes.front: For 2025, the deduction for qualified passenger vehicle loan interest is up to {{c1::$10,000}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of the four Schedule 1-A deductions.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on car loan interest”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: you may be eligible to deduct up to $10,000 of that interest.

notes.front: For the 2025 car loan interest deduction, when and for what use must the vehicle have been bought?
notes.back: Bought in 2025, for personal use.
notes.explanation: Interest on a vehicle bought in another year, or not for personal use, falls outside this rule.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on car loan interest”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: If you paid or accrued qualified passenger vehicle loan interest on a vehicle you purchased in 2025 for personal use

notes.front: Above what modified AGI is the car loan interest deduction limited?
notes.back: $100,000 ($200,000 if married filing jointly).
notes.explanation: These levels are lower than those for the tips and overtime deductions.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on car loan interest”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Your deduction will be limited if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $100,000 ($200,000 if married filing jointly).

notes.front: Ana, single, modified AGI $70,000, bought a car for personal use in March 2025 and paid $11,500 of qualifying loan interest that year. What can she deduct?
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the cap. C: she meets the purchase-year and use rules and is under $100,000.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on car loan interest”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: you may be eligible to deduct up to $10,000 of that interest.

notes.front: Ben bought his personal car in 2023 and paid loan interest on it in 2025. Can he claim the car loan interest deduction for 2025?
notes.back: B: no; the vehicle must have been purchased in 2025.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, up to $10,000
B) No
C) Yes, but only half
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the purchase-year condition is not met, so no amount is allowed.
notes.explanation: A 2023 purchase fails the purchase-year condition, whatever the vehicle is used for.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on car loan interest”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: If you paid or accrued qualified passenger vehicle loan interest on a vehicle you purchased in 2025 for personal use

notes.front: A single taxpayer with modified AGI of $120,000 paid $4,000 of qualifying car loan interest in 2025. What happens?
notes.back: C: the deduction is limited because modified AGI exceeds $100,000.
notes.choices:
A) Deduct $4,000 in full
B) No deduction, as it is over $10,000
C) The deduction is limited
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the income limit. C confuses the interest cap with the income threshold.
notes.explanation: $120,000 is more than the $100,000 single threshold, so the deduction is reduced.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: No tax on car loan interest”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Your deduction will be limited if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $100,000 ($200,000 if married filing jointly).

notes.front: What is the most the 2025 enhanced senior deduction can be?
notes.back: $6,000, or $12,000 if both spouses are eligible.
notes.explanation: Each eligible spouse brings their own $6,000.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Enhanced deduction for seniors”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The maximum amount of the deduction is $6,000 ($12,000 if both spouses are eligible).

notes.front: To be eligible for the 2025 enhanced senior deduction, you must have been born before {{c1::January 2, 1961}}.
notes.back: January 2, 1961
notes.explanation: This is the same birth-date test Pub. 501 uses for the higher standard deduction for age.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Enhanced deduction for seniors”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: If you were born before January 2, 1961, you may be eligible for an enhanced senior deduction.

notes.front: Above what modified AGI is the enhanced senior deduction limited?
notes.back: $75,000 ($150,000 if married filing jointly).
notes.explanation: These are the lowest income levels of the four Schedule 1-A deductions.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Enhanced deduction for seniors”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Your deduction will be limited if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $75,000 ($150,000 if married filing jointly).

notes.front: A couple filing jointly, both born in 1957, has modified AGI of $90,000 and valid social security numbers. What is their enhanced senior deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: A counts only one spouse. C: they are under the $150,000 joint threshold.
notes.explanation: Both spouses eligible: $6,000 × 2 = $12,000; $90,000 < $150,000, so no reduction.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Enhanced deduction for seniors”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The maximum amount of the deduction is $6,000 ($12,000 if both spouses are eligible).

notes.front: A joint-filing couple has one spouse born in 1959 and one born in 1966; modified AGI is $100,000. What is the enhanced senior deduction?
notes.back: A: $6,000, for the spouse born before 2 January 1961.
notes.choicesExplained: B counts the younger spouse, who is not eligible. C: one spouse qualifies.
notes.explanation: Only one spouse meets the birth-date test: $6,000; $100,000 < $150,000.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Enhanced deduction for seniors”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: If you were born before January 2, 1961, you may be eligible for an enhanced senior deduction.

notes.front: Harold, born in 1955, is married and files separately for 2025. Can he take the enhanced senior deduction?
notes.back: B: no; married taxpayers must file jointly to claim it.
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: no amount is allowed on a separate return.
notes.explanation: Being old enough is not enough: a married senior needs a joint return.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Enhanced deduction for seniors”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: To be eligible, you and/or your spouse must have a valid SSN. If you are married, you must file a joint return. The maximum amount of the deduction

notes.front: Irene is single, born in 1950, with modified AGI of $95,000. What happens to her enhanced senior deduction?
notes.back: C: it is limited, since $95,000 exceeds $75,000.
notes.choices:
A) $6,000 in full
B) $12,000
C) It is limited
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the income limit. C is the two-spouse maximum.
notes.explanation: $95,000 − $75,000 = $20,000 over the single threshold, so the deduction is reduced.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Enhanced deduction for seniors”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Your deduction will be limited if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $75,000 ($150,000 if married filing jointly).

notes.front: On Schedule A you can deduct only the part of medical and dental expenses that is more than {{c1::7.5%}} of AGI.
notes.explanation: Expenses up to that level of AGI give no deduction.
notes.source: Publication 502 (2025), Medical and Dental Expenses, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: only the part of your medical and dental expenses that is more than 7.5% of your adjusted gross income (AGI).

notes.front: How does Pub. 502 define medical expenses?
notes.back: The costs of diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention of disease, and for affecting any part or function of the body.
notes.explanation: They include payments to physicians, surgeons, dentists and other medical practitioners.
notes.source: Publication 502 (2025), Medical and Dental Expenses, “What Are Medical Expenses?”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Medical expenses are the costs of diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease and for the purpose of affecting any part or function of the body.

notes.front: Which year’s medical expenses can you include on a 2025 return?
notes.back: Only those you paid in 2025, generally not payments for care you will receive in a future year.
notes.explanation: Pub. 502 notes an exception for a decedent’s expenses.
notes.source: Publication 502 (2025), Medical and Dental Expenses, “What Expenses Can You Include This Year?”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: You can include only the medical and dental expenses you paid this year but generally not payments for medical or dental care you will receive in a future year.

notes.front: Nadia itemizes. Her AGI is $80,000 and she paid $9,000 of unreimbursed medical expenses in 2025. How much is deductible?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the AGI floor. C is the floor itself, not the excess.
notes.source: Publication 502 (2025), Medical and Dental Expenses, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: only the part of your medical and dental expenses that is more than 7.5% of your adjusted gross income (AGI).

notes.front: Do medical expenses include long-term care?
notes.back: Yes: qualified long-term care services, and limited amounts of qualified long-term care insurance premiums.
notes.explanation: The premiums are included only up to limits, unlike the services.
notes.source: Publication 502 (2025), Medical and Dental Expenses, “What Are Medical Expenses?”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Medical expenses also include amounts paid for qualified long-term care services and limited amounts paid for any qualified long-term care insurance contract.

notes.front: The 2025 standard mileage rate for using your car for medical reasons is {{c1::21 cents}} a mile.
notes.back: 21 cents
notes.explanation: You can use it instead of actual car expenses.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Reminders: Standard mileage rate”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: The 2025 rate for operating expenses for a car when you use it for medical reasons is 21 cents a mile.

notes.front: Luis drove 1,500 miles for medical care in 2025 and paid $40 in parking. Using the standard rate, how much goes into his medical expenses?
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves out parking. C uses the 70-cent business rate.
notes.explanation: Miles × 21 cents gives $315 (1,500 × $0.21); parking fees and tolls are then added on top.
notes.source: Publication 502 (2025), Medical and Dental Expenses, “Transportation”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: you can use the standard medical mileage rate of 21 cents a mile. You can also include parking fees and tolls.

notes.front: The 2025 rate for using your car for volunteer work for certain charitable organizations is {{c1::14 cents}} a mile.
notes.back: 14 cents
notes.explanation: It is lower than both the medical (21 cents) and business (70 cents) rates.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Reminders: Standard mileage rate”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: The 2025 rate for use of your vehicle to do volunteer work for certain charitable organizations is 14 cents a mile.

notes.front: What is the 2025 overall limit on the deduction for state and local income, sales and property taxes?
notes.back: $40,000 ($20,000 if married filing separately).
notes.explanation: The limit was increased for 2025.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: State and local tax deduction limit increased”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The overall limit on the deduction for state and local income, sales, and property taxes has increased to $40,000 ($20,000 if married filing separately).

notes.front: When is the 2025 state and local tax limit reduced, and how low can it go?
notes.back: When modified AGI exceeds $500,000 ($250,000 married filing separately); not below $10,000 ($5,000 married filing separately).
notes.explanation: The reduction has a floor, so some deduction always remains.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: State and local tax deduction limit increased”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The overall limit is reduced if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $500,000 ($250,000 if married filing separately) but will not be reduced below $10,000 ($5,000 if married filing separately).

notes.front: Ellen is single, AGI $180,000, and paid $28,000 of state income tax and $17,000 of property tax in 2025. How much state and local tax can she deduct?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the limit. C is the floor that applies only above $500,000 of modified AGI.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: State and local tax deduction limit increased”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The overall limit on the deduction for state and local income, sales, and property taxes has increased to $40,000 ($20,000 if married filing separately).

notes.front: A couple filing jointly has modified AGI of $900,000. What is the lowest their 2025 state and local tax limit can fall to?
notes.choicesExplained: A: the limit has a floor. B is the floor for married filing separately.
notes.explanation: Above $500,000 the $40,000 limit is reduced, but not below $10,000.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: State and local tax deduction limit increased”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: but will not be reduced below $10,000 ($5,000 if married filing separately).

notes.front: For home acquisition debt taken out after 15 December 2017, mortgage interest is deductible on the first how much of debt?
notes.back: $750,000 ($375,000 if married filing separately).
notes.explanation: Older debt keeps a higher limit.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: mortgage interest on the first $750,000 ($375,000 if married filing separately) of indebtedness.

notes.front: What limit applies to mortgage interest on debt incurred before 16 December 2017?
notes.back: $1 million ($500,000 if married filing separately).
notes.explanation: The higher limit is kept for debt from before the change.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: higher limitations ($1 million ($500,000 if married filing separately)) apply if you are deducting mortgage interest from indebtedness incurred before December 16, 2017.

notes.front: Do the mortgage debt limits apply to each home separately?
notes.back: No: they apply to the combined mortgages on your main home and second home.
notes.explanation: A second home does not bring a second limit.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Part I: Fully deductible interest”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: The dollar limits for the second and third categories apply to the combined mortgages on your main home and second home.

notes.front: In 2020 the Parks, filing jointly, took a $900,000 mortgage to buy their main home. Is all 2025 interest on it deductible?
notes.back: C: only the part on the first $750,000.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it is under $1 million
B) No, none of it
C) No, only the interest on the first $750,000 of debt
notes.choicesExplained: A applies the pre-2017 limit to a 2020 loan. B: interest on debt up to the limit is deductible.
notes.explanation: Debt after 15 December 2017 → $750,000 limit; $900,000 exceeds it by $150,000.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: mortgage interest on the first $750,000 ($375,000 if married filing separately) of indebtedness.

notes.front: The Okafors, filing jointly, took a $900,000 mortgage in 2015 to buy their home. Which limit applies to their 2025 interest?
notes.back: B: $1 million, so all the interest is within the limit.
notes.choicesExplained: A is for debt after 15 December 2017. C is the married-filing-separately figure for later debt.
notes.explanation: Debt from 2015 is before 16 December 2017; $900,000 is under $1 million.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: higher limitations ($1 million ($500,000 if married filing separately)) apply if you are deducting mortgage interest from indebtedness incurred before December 16, 2017.

notes.front: What other name may points go by?
notes.back: Loan origination fees.
notes.explanation: The name does not change what the charge is.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Points”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Points may also be called loan origination fees

notes.front: If you don’t deduct points in full in the year paid, how may you deduct them?
notes.back: Ratably (equally) over the life of the loan, if you meet the tests.
notes.explanation: Pub. 936 lists tests for this, starting with using the cash method of accounting.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Deduction Allowed Ratably”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: you can deduct the points ratably (equally) over the life of the loan if you meet all of the following tests.

notes.front: Sam chose not to deduct $3,600 of points on a 30-year mortgage in the year paid and meets the tests for spreading them. How much per year?
notes.back: A: $120 a year.
notes.choicesExplained: A is the full deduction in the year paid, which he chose not to take. C spreads them over 10 years, not 30.
notes.explanation: $3,600 ÷ 30 years = $120 a year, deducted equally over the loan’s life.
notes.source: Publication 936 (2025), Home Mortgage Interest Deduction, “Deduction Allowed Ratably”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: you can deduct the points ratably (equally) over the life of the loan if you meet all of the following tests.

notes.front: What limits the deduction for investment interest expense, and what happens to the excess?
notes.back: Net investment income limits it; the excess carries over to the next tax year.
notes.explanation: The carried-over interest is treated as paid in that next year.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Limit on Deduction”, PDF p. 47
notes.evidence: Generally, your deduction for investment interest expense is limited to your net investment income. You can carry over the amount of investment interest you could not deduct because of this limit to the next tax year.

notes.front: Farah paid $5,000 of investment interest in 2025 and had $3,000 of net investment income. What happens?
notes.back: B: deduct $3,000; carry $2,000 forward.
notes.choices:
A) Deduct $5,000
B) Deduct $3,000 and carry $2,000 to 2026
C) Deduct $3,000 and lose $2,000
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the limit. C: the excess is carried over, not lost.
notes.explanation: $5,000 − $3,000 limit = $2,000 carried to the next year.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Limit on Deduction”, PDF p. 47
notes.evidence: Generally, your deduction for investment interest expense is limited to your net investment income. You can carry over the amount of investment interest you could not deduct because of this limit to the next tax year.

notes.front: When debt is used for several purposes, which interest counts as investment interest?
notes.back: Only the interest on the part of the debt used for investment purposes.
notes.explanation: The debt is allocated by use, not by the property securing it.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Allocation of interest expense”, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: If you borrow money for business, personal purposes, or investment, you must allocate the debt among those purposes. Only the interest expense on the part of the debt used for investment purposes is treated as investment expense.

notes.front: What is the general limit on the charitable contribution deduction?
notes.back: 60% of AGI, though in some cases a 20%, 30% or 50% limit may apply.
notes.explanation: The limit that applies depends on the property given and the organization receiving it.
notes.source: Publication 526 (2025), Charitable Contributions, “Introduction”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Your deduction for charitable contributions generally can't be more than 60% of your AGI, but in some cases 20%, 30%, or 50% limits may apply.

notes.front: Besides 60%, which three percentage-of-AGI limits can apply to charitable contributions?
notes.back: 50%, 30% and 20% of AGI.
notes.explanation: Which one applies depends on the type of property and the type of organization.
notes.source: Publication 526 (2025), Charitable Contributions, “Limits on Deductions”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Your deduction may be further limited to 50%, 30%, or 20% of your AGI, depending on the type of property you give and the type of organization you give it to.

notes.front: Hana’s AGI is $50,000. In 2025 she gave $35,000 in cash to her church and made no other gifts. How much can she deduct?
notes.back: B: $30,000; the other $5,000 may be carried over.
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the 60% limit. C uses 50%.
notes.source: Publication 526 (2025), Charitable Contributions, “Limits on Deductions”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Your deduction for cash contributions is limited to 60% of your AGI minus your deductions for all other contributions.

notes.front: For how many later years can you carry over charitable contributions that exceed the AGI limits?
notes.back: Each of the next 5 years (15 years for a qualified conservation contribution).
notes.explanation: After that time, any unused excess is lost.
notes.source: Publication 526 (2025), Charitable Contributions, “Carryovers”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: Except for qualified conservation contributions, you may be able to deduct the excess in each of the next 5 years until it is used up, but not beyond that time.

notes.front: What record do you need to deduct a single contribution of $250 or more?
notes.back: A contemporaneous written acknowledgment from the organization (or certain payroll deduction records).
notes.explanation: Without it, the deduction for that contribution is not allowed.
notes.source: Publication 526 (2025), Charitable Contributions, “Contributions of $250 or More”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: You can claim a deduction for a contribution of $250 or more only if you have a contemporaneous written acknowledgment of your contribution from the qualified organization, or certain payroll deduction records.

notes.front: In testing for the $250 rule, do you add up separate contributions to the same charity?
notes.back: No: separate contributions are not combined.
notes.explanation: Pub. 526 gives weekly gifts to a church as an example that are tested one by one.
notes.source: Publication 526 (2025), Charitable Contributions, “Amount of contribution”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: In figuring whether your contribution is $250 or more, don't combine separate contributions.

notes.front: In 2025 Ivy gave her temple $40 each week, plus one $400 cheque in December. Which gift needs a written acknowledgment?
notes.back: A: only the single $400 cheque.
notes.choices:
A) Only the $400 cheque
B) Every weekly $40 gift
C) The weekly gifts, because they total $2,080
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: each weekly gift is under $250, and separate contributions aren’t combined.
notes.explanation: $400 ≥ $250 needs an acknowledgment; each $40 gift is tested alone.
notes.source: Publication 526 (2025), Charitable Contributions, “Amount of contribution”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: In figuring whether your contribution is $250 or more, don't combine separate contributions.

notes.front: For tax years after 2017, when are casualty and theft losses of personal-use property deductible?
notes.back: Only when the loss is attributable to a federally declared disaster.
notes.explanation: Pub. 547 limits this to property not connected with a trade or business or a profit-seeking transaction.
notes.source: Publication 547 (2025), Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts, “Limitation on personal casualty and theft losses”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: casualty or theft losses of personal-use property not connected with a trade or business or a transaction entered into for profit are deductible only if the loss is attributable to a federally declared disaster.

notes.front: How much is each personal casualty or theft loss reduced by before the AGI limit?
notes.back: $100 per event, however many items are involved.
notes.explanation: Only one $100 reduction applies to a single event.
notes.source: Publication 547 (2025), Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts, “$100 Rule”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: It doesn't matter how many pieces of property are involved in an event. Only a single $100 reduction applies.

notes.front: After the $100 reduction, by how much is a total personal casualty loss from a federally declared disaster reduced?
notes.back: By 10% of AGI.
notes.explanation: The 10% rule applies to the year’s total, after each loss is reduced by $100.
notes.source: Publication 547 (2025), Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts, “10% Rule”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: total casualty or theft loss attributable to a federally declared disaster by 10% of your AGI. Apply this rule to personal-use property after you reduce each loss by $100 (the $100 rule).

notes.front: A federally declared flood destroyed Pia’s furniture: a $20,000 loss after insurance. Her AGI is $60,000. What is her casualty loss deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: A applies neither reduction. B applies only the $100 rule.
notes.source: Publication 547 (2025), Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts, “10% Rule”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: total casualty or theft loss attributable to a federally declared disaster by 10% of your AGI. Apply this rule to personal-use property after you reduce each loss by $100 (the $100 rule).

notes.front: In 2025 thieves took $5,000 of jewellery from Adam’s home. There was no federally declared disaster. Can he deduct the loss as an itemized deduction?
notes.back: A: generally no; a personal theft loss must be attributable to a federally declared disaster.
notes.choices:
A) Generally no
B) Yes, after the $100 and 10% rules
C) Yes, in full
notes.choicesExplained: B and C apply the reductions to a loss that is not deductible to begin with.
notes.explanation: For tax years after 2017, the federally declared disaster condition is not met here.
notes.source: Publication 547 (2025), Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts, “Limitation on personal casualty and theft losses”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: casualty or theft losses of personal-use property not connected with a trade or business or a transaction entered into for profit are deductible only if the loss is attributable to a federally declared disaster.

notes.front: Which nonresident aliens can claim itemized deductions?
notes.back: Only those with income effectively connected with their trade or business in the United States.
notes.explanation: They can claim some, not all, of the itemized deductions resident aliens can claim.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Itemized Deductions”, PDF p. 39
notes.evidence: Nonresident aliens can claim some of the same itemized deductions that resident aliens can claim. However, nonresident aliens can claim itemized deductions only if they have income effectively connected with their U.S. trade or business.

notes.front: Up to what share of net QBI from a trade or business can the QBI deduction be?
notes.back: Up to 20%.
notes.explanation: It can include income from a pass-through entity but not from a C corporation.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025), Qualified Business Income Deduction Simplified Computation, “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: may be entitled to a deduction of up to 20% of their net QBI from a trade or business, including income from a pass-through entity, but not from a C corporation

notes.front: Is income from performing services as an employee QBI?
notes.back: No: performing services as an employee is not a qualified trade or business.
notes.explanation: Nor are trades or businesses conducted by corporations.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025), Qualified Business Income Deduction Simplified Computation, “Trade or business”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: trades or businesses conducted by corporations and the performance of services as an employee aren't qualified trades or businesses.

notes.front: Ruth earns $60,000 of wages as an employee and $30,000 of net profit from a sole proprietorship. Which is QBI?
notes.back: B: only the sole proprietorship profit.
notes.choices:
A) Both
B) Only the $30,000 business profit
C) Only the wages
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: employee services aren’t a qualified trade or business.
notes.explanation: Performing services as an employee is not a qualified trade or business, so the $60,000 of wages is not QBI; only the $30,000 profit is.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025), Qualified Business Income Deduction Simplified Computation, “Trade or business”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: trades or businesses conducted by corporations and the performance of services as an employee aren't qualified trades or businesses.

notes.front: Up to what 2025 taxable income (before the QBI deduction) can you use the simplified Form 8995?
notes.back: $197,300, or $394,600 if married filing jointly; above that, Form 8995-A.
notes.explanation: The income is measured before the QBI deduction itself.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025), Qualified Business Income Deduction Simplified Computation, “Who Can Use Form 8995”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: your 2025 taxable income before your QBI deduction is less than or equal to $394,600 if married filing jointly, and $197,300 for all other returns

notes.front: Omari is single, with a sole proprietorship and 2025 taxable income of $210,000 before the QBI deduction. Which form figures his deduction?
notes.back: B: Form 8995-A.
notes.choices:
A) Form 8995
B) Form 8995-A
C) Schedule 1-A
notes.choicesExplained: A is only for taxable income up to $197,300 (single). C holds the new 2025 deductions, not QBI.
notes.explanation: $210,000 > $197,300, so the simplified form can’t be used.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025), Qualified Business Income Deduction Simplified Computation, “Who Can Use Form 8995”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: If your income is more than the threshold, you must use Form 8995-A.

notes.front: Mina, single, runs a consulting practice (a specified service trade or business). Her 2025 taxable income before the QBI deduction is $150,000. Does her practice count?
notes.back: C: yes; at or below $197,300 it is treated as a qualified trade or business.
notes.choices:
A) Only partly
B) No, never
C) Yes, as a qualified trade or business
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the income exception. C applies only in the phase-in range above $197,300.
notes.explanation: $150,000 ≤ $197,300, so Exception 1 applies.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025), Qualified Business Income Deduction Simplified Computation, “Exception 1”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: if your 2025 taxable income before the QBI deduction is less than or equal to $394,600 if married filing jointly, and $197,300 for all others, your SSTB is treated as a qualified trade or business.

notes.front: What is the 2025 phase-in range in which only a percentage of a specified service business counts for QBI?
notes.back: Taxable income over $197,300 up to $247,300 ($394,600 to $494,600 if married filing jointly).
notes.explanation: Within the range, Schedule A of Form 8995-A is used.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025), Qualified Business Income Deduction Simplified Computation, “Exception 2”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: is more than $197,300 but not more than $247,300 for all other returns, an applicable percentage of your SSTB is treated as a qualified trade or business

notes.front: The expense limit for the 2025 child and dependent care credit with one qualifying person is {{c1::$3,000}}.
notes.explanation: The limit doubles with two or more qualifying persons.
notes.source: Publication 503 (2025), Child and Dependent Care Expenses, “Introduction”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: dollar limit for qualifying expenses (generally, $3,000 if you had one qualifying person or $6,000 if you had two or more qualifying persons)

notes.front: The expense limit for the child and dependent care credit with two or more qualifying persons is {{c1::$6,000}}.
notes.explanation: It is twice the one-person limit.
notes.source: Publication 503 (2025), Child and Dependent Care Expenses, “Introduction”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: $3,000 if you had one qualifying person or $6,000 if you had two or more qualifying persons

notes.front: Up to what share of employment-related expenses can the child and dependent care credit be?
notes.back: Up to 35%.
notes.explanation: The expenses must be paid so you (and your spouse, if joint) can work or look for work.
notes.source: Publication 503 (2025), Child and Dependent Care Expenses, “Introduction”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: The credit can be up to 35% of your employment-related expenses. To qualify, you must pay these expenses so you (or your spouse if filing jointly) can work or look for work.

notes.front: Zara paid $5,000 of day care for her one qualifying child in 2025 so she could work. What expense amount counts toward the credit?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the limit. C is the limit for two or more qualifying persons.
notes.explanation: One qualifying person → $3,000 limit; $5,000 is capped at $3,000.
notes.source: Publication 503 (2025), Child and Dependent Care Expenses, “Introduction”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: dollar limit for qualifying expenses (generally, $3,000 if you had one qualifying person or $6,000 if you had two or more qualifying persons)

notes.front: The Dubois pay $7,500 of after-school care for their two qualifying children so both can work. What amount counts?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the limit. C is the one-person limit.
notes.explanation: Two or more qualifying persons → $6,000 limit; $7,500 is capped at $6,000.
notes.source: Publication 503 (2025), Child and Dependent Care Expenses, “Introduction”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: $3,000 if you had one qualifying person or $6,000 if you had two or more qualifying persons

notes.front: For 2025 the maximum child tax credit for each qualifying child is {{c1::$2,200}}.
notes.explanation: The amount increased for 2025.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “What’s New: CTC amount increased”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The maximum amount of CTC for each qualifying child increased to $2,200.

notes.front: For 2025 the maximum additional child tax credit for each qualifying child is {{c1::$1,700}}.
notes.explanation: It is lower than the $2,200 maximum child tax credit.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “Reminders: ACTC amount”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The maximum amount of ACTC for each qualifying child is $1,700.

notes.front: From 2025, who needs a valid social security number to claim the CTC or ACTC on a joint return?
notes.back: Only one spouse; the other needs a social security number or individual taxpayer identification number issued by the due date.
notes.explanation: On a return without that, neither credit can be claimed, even on an amended return.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “SSN required before the due date of your return”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: If you are filing a joint return, only one spouse is required to have a valid SSN to be eligible for the CTC or ACTC. The other spouse must have either an SSN or ITIN, and it must have been issued on or before the due date of the return.

notes.front: Above what modified AGI does the CTC begin to phase out for filing statuses other than married filing jointly?
notes.explanation: Modified AGI for this is line 3 of Schedule 8812.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “Modified AGI”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: • All other filing statuses –$200,000 Modified AGI. For purposes of the CTC and ODC, your modified AGI is the amount on line 3 of Schedule 8812.

notes.front: Above what modified AGI does the CTC begin to phase out for married filing jointly?
notes.explanation: It is twice the $200,000 level for other statuses.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “Modified AGI”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Married filing jointly –$400,000 • All other filing statuses –$200,000

notes.front: Can you claim both the CTC and the ODC for the same person?
notes.back: No: you can’t check both boxes for the same person.
notes.explanation: Each dependent brings one credit or the other.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “Line 4”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: You can't check both the child tax credit box and the credit for other dependents box for the same person.

notes.front: For the child tax credit, how old must the qualifying child be?
notes.back: Under age 17 at the end of the year, and claimed as your dependent.
notes.explanation: An older dependent child may qualify you for the ODC instead.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Child tax credit”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: you may be entitled to a child tax credit for each qualifying child who was under age 17 at the end of the year if you claimed that child as a dependent.

notes.front: A head of household with one qualifying child has modified AGI of $230,000. What happens to the CTC?
notes.back: A: it phases out, since $230,000 exceeds $200,000.
notes.choices:
A) It begins to phase out
B) Full $2,200
C) No credit at all for head of household
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the threshold. C: head of household can claim the credit.
notes.explanation: $230,000 − $200,000 = $30,000 over the threshold for statuses other than joint.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “Modified AGI”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: • All other filing statuses –$200,000 Modified AGI. For purposes of the CTC and ODC, your modified AGI is the amount on line 3 of Schedule 8812.

notes.front: A couple filing jointly has modified AGI of $390,000 and two qualifying children. Is their CTC reduced by the phase-out?
notes.back: C: no reduction; $390,000 is under $400,000.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, above $200,000
B) Yes, it is fully lost
C) No, it is under $400,000
notes.choicesExplained: A uses the threshold for other statuses. B: they are below the joint threshold.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “Modified AGI”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Married filing jointly –$400,000 • All other filing statuses –$200,000

notes.front: Olga’s dependent son turned 17 in 2025 and lives with her. Which credit can he bring her?
notes.back: A: the ODC, since he is not under 17 at the end of the year.
notes.choices:
A) Credit for other dependents of up to $500
B) Child tax credit of $2,200
C) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: B: the CTC needs a child under 17 at year end. C: a dependent may still bring the ODC.
notes.explanation: Age 17 at year end fails the CTC age test; the ODC is up to $500.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Child tax credit”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: you may be entitled to a child tax credit for each qualifying child who was under age 17 at the end of the year if you claimed that child as a dependent.

notes.front: The Morales family owes no income tax for 2025 and has one qualifying child. Which statement fits the child credit?
notes.back: A: up to $1,700 may come as the refundable ACTC.
notes.choices:
A) Up to $1,700 may be received as the ACTC
B) Nothing can be received, as the credit is nonrefundable
C) The full $2,200 is refunded
notes.choicesExplained: B: the ACTC is the part that can be refunded. C: the ACTC maximum per child is $1,700, not $2,200.
notes.explanation: With no tax to offset, only the ACTC portion (max $1,700 per child) can be received.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040) (2025), “Reminders: ACTC amount”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The maximum amount of ACTC for each qualifying child is $1,700.

notes.front: For returns properly claiming the ACTC, when is the earliest the refund can be issued?
notes.back: Mid-February 2026, and the delay applies to the entire refund.
notes.explanation: Not just the part linked to the ACTC is held.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Reminders: Delayed refund for returns claiming the ACTC”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: The IRS cannot issue refunds before mid-February 2026 for returns that properly claim the ACTC. This time frame applies to the entire refund, not just the portion associated with the ACTC.

notes.front: From 2025, what identification must the taxpayer (or spouse on a joint return) have to claim the ODC?
notes.back: A valid social security number or individual taxpayer identification number issued by the return’s due date, including extensions.
notes.explanation: A number issued after the due date does not qualify.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Credit for other dependents”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: must have a valid SSN or ITIN issued on or before the due date of your return (including extensions).

notes.front: Femi supports his widowed mother, who is his dependent (qualifying relative) and has a valid social security number. Which credit may he claim for her?
notes.back: A: the ODC of up to $500.
notes.choices:
A) Credit for other dependents, up to $500
B) Child tax credit
C) No credit
notes.choicesExplained: B: she is not a qualifying child under 17. C: an eligible dependent can bring the ODC.
notes.explanation: The ODC may reduce tax by up to $500 for each eligible dependent.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Child Tax Credit and Credit for Other Dependents”, PDF p. 111
notes.evidence: The ODC is a credit that may reduce your tax by as much as $500 for each eligible dependent.

notes.front: The maximum 2025 American opportunity credit is {{c1::$2,500}} per eligible student.
notes.explanation: It is per student, unlike the lifetime learning credit, which is per return.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Table 2-1. Overview of the American Opportunity Credit”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Maximum credit Up to $2,500 credit per eligible student

notes.front: The maximum 2025 lifetime learning credit is {{c1::$2,000}} per return.
notes.explanation: It covers all eligible students on the return together.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Table 3-1. Overview of the Lifetime Learning Credit”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Maximum credit Up to $2,000 credit per return

notes.front: What share of the American opportunity credit may be refundable?
notes.back: 40%, limited to $1,000 per student.
notes.explanation: The rest is nonrefundable.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Appendix B”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: 40% of the credit may be refundable (limited to $1,000 per student)

notes.front: Yusuf qualifies for a $2,500 AOTC for his daughter but owes no tax. How much can be refunded to him?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the refundable part. C: only 40% may be refundable.
notes.explanation: 40% × $2,500 = $1,000, which is also the per-student cap.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Appendix B”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: 40% of the credit may be refundable (limited to $1,000 per student)

notes.front: Over what 2025 modified AGI range does the AOTC phase out?
notes.explanation: Above the top of the range no credit is allowed.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Effect of the Amount of Your Income on the Amount of Your Credit”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: is phased out (gradually reduced) if your MAGI is between $80,000 and $90,000 ($160,000 and $180,000 if you file a joint return). You can't claim an American opportunity credit if your MAGI is $90,000 or more

notes.front: Over what 2025 modified AGI range does the lifetime learning credit phase out?
notes.explanation: For 2025 the range is the same as the AOTC’s.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Effect of the Amount of Your Income on the Amount of Your Credit”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: The amount of your lifetime learning credit is phased out (gradually reduced) if your MAGI is between $80,000 and $90,000 ($160,000 and $180,000 if you file a joint return).

notes.front: Chen is single with 2025 modified AGI of $95,000 and a daughter in her first year of college. How much AOTC can he claim?
notes.back: A: none, since his modified AGI is $90,000 or more.
notes.choices:
A) None
B) A reduced amount
C) $2,500
notes.choicesExplained: C and B apply only below $90,000.
notes.explanation: $95,000 ≥ $90,000 → no American opportunity credit.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Effect of the Amount of Your Income on the Amount of Your Credit”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: You can't claim an American opportunity credit if your MAGI is $90,000 or more

notes.front: Gina, single, has 2025 modified AGI of $85,000 and pays for a night-school course. What happens to her lifetime learning credit?
notes.back: B: reduced; $85,000 is inside the $80,000–$90,000 range.
notes.choices:
A) Full credit
B) Reduced credit
C) No credit
notes.choicesExplained: A applies below $80,000. C applies at $90,000 or more.
notes.explanation: $85,000 is halfway through the $10,000 single range.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Effect of the Amount of Your Income on the Amount of Your Credit”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: The amount of your lifetime learning credit is phased out (gradually reduced) if your MAGI is between $80,000 and $90,000

notes.front: What form must the student generally have received from the school to claim the AOTC or LLC?
notes.back: Form 1098-T from an eligible educational institution, domestic or foreign.
notes.explanation: There are exceptions when the school isn’t required to furnish one.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Form 1098-T requirement”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: the law requires a taxpayer (or a dependent) to have received Form 1098-T from an eligible educational institution, whether domestic or foreign.

notes.front: How do the AOTC and the LLC differ in the number of years they can be claimed for the same student?
notes.back: AOTC: no more than 4 tax years. LLC: no limit.
notes.explanation: Pub. 970 lists this among the differences between the two credits.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Can You Claim More Than One Education Credit This Year?”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: you can claim the American opportunity credit based on the same student's expenses for no more than 4 tax years. However, there is no limit on the number of years for which you can claim a lifetime learning credit

notes.front: Kai, a dependent, is in his sixth year of university (a master’s course) and his parents already claimed the AOTC for him for 4 years. Which credit can they consider?
notes.back: B: the lifetime learning credit.
notes.choices:
A) AOTC again
B) Lifetime learning credit
C) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: A: the AOTC is limited to 4 tax years per student. C: the LLC has no year limit.
notes.explanation: Four AOTC years are used up; the LLC can be claimed for any number of years.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Can You Claim More Than One Education Credit This Year?”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: However, there is no limit on the number of years for which you can claim a lifetime learning credit based on the same student's expenses.

notes.front: The Haddads have two children in their second year of college, each qualifying for the AOTC in full. What is the most AOTC they can claim?
notes.choicesExplained: A treats the AOTC as per return. B uses the lifetime learning credit figure twice.
notes.explanation: $2,500 per eligible student × 2 = $5,000.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Table 2-1. Overview of the American Opportunity Credit”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Maximum credit Up to $2,500 credit per eligible student

notes.front: Can you take a credit for some foreign taxes and a deduction for others in the same year?
notes.back: Generally no: each year you choose a credit or a deduction for all qualified foreign taxes.
notes.explanation: The choice covers all qualified foreign taxes paid or accrued that year.
notes.source: Publication 514 (2025), Foreign Tax Credit for Individuals, “Choosing To Take Credit or Deduction”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: As a general rule, you must choose each year to take either a credit or a deduction for all qualified foreign taxes paid or accrued in that year.

notes.front: Aiko paid $1,200 of qualified foreign income tax. Which choice reduces her United States tax liability directly, not just her taxable income?
notes.back: A: the foreign tax credit.
notes.choices:
A) Foreign tax credit
B) Deduction on Schedule A
C) Either, with the same effect
notes.choicesExplained: A reduces taxable income, not tax. C: the two work differently.
notes.explanation: As a credit, foreign income taxes reduce tax liability; as a deduction, taxable income.
notes.source: Publication 514 (2025), Foreign Tax Credit for Individuals, “Introduction”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Taken as a deduction, foreign income taxes reduce your U.S. taxable income. Taken as a credit, foreign income taxes reduce your U.S. tax liability.

notes.front: For 2025, investment income must be {{c1::$11,950}} or less to claim the EIC.
notes.explanation: It is one of the rules everyone claiming the EIC must meet.
notes.source: Publication 596 (2025), Earned Income Credit, “Rule 6”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Rule 6—Your Investment Income Must Be $11,950 or Less

notes.front: Marta’s 2025 earned income is $30,000 and she has $12,400 of dividends and interest. Can she claim the EIC?
notes.back: A: no; her investment income is over $11,950.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes
notes.choicesExplained: B: the investment income limit is a rule for everyone, whatever the earned income.
notes.source: Publication 596 (2025), Earned Income Credit, “Rule 6”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Rule 6—Your Investment Income Must Be $11,950 or Less

notes.front: What is the 2025 EIC earned income limit with three or more qualifying children?
notes.back: Less than $61,555 ($68,675 if married filing jointly).
notes.explanation: This is the highest of the four limits.
notes.source: Publication 596 (2025), Earned Income Credit, “What’s New”, PDF p. 3
